lead: Every beam section has a balance point called the centroid. The area spread about that point is measured by the second moment of area, I. Together they fix the neutral axis and the bending stiffness of the section. A deep I-section carries more bending moment than a flat strip of the same area because its material sits far from the neutral axis. This chapter shows how to find the centroid of a composite area, how to compute I about centroidal axes, and how to use the parallel-axis theorem. These numbers feed directly into the bending formula in 4.2.
prereq: You need: basic statics from Unit 3, Shear Force and Bending Moment.

sections.h3: Centroid and first moment of area

blocks.text: The centroid of an area is the point where a thin uniform sheet of that shape would balance. For a section in the x-y plane, write the centroid as (x̄, ȳ). The first moment of area about the x-axis is Q_x = Σ A_i y_i, and about the y-axis is Q_y = Σ A_i x_i. Here A_i is the area of part i in mm², and (x_i, y_i) is its centroid in mm. First moments carry units of mm³.
x̄ = Σ A_i x_i / Σ A_i,    ȳ = Σ A_i y_i / Σ A_i
blocks.where: x̄, ȳ are centroid coordinates in mm; A_i is each part area in mm²; x_i, y_i are each part centroid in mm; Σ A_i is total area in mm².

blocks.text: For a composite section, split it into simple rectangles, circles or triangles. Choose an origin and positive directions first. Find each part area and its own centroid from the base. Multiply area by centroid distance, add, and divide by total area. A hole is a negative area: subtract both its area and its first moment. For the second moment, a hole is also subtracted in full: subtract (I_c of the hole + A d² for the hole) about the required axis. Always state where ȳ is measured from, because the same section has different ȳ values from the top and from the bottom.

items: Draw the section and choose x and y axes.
Split into simple parts; label holes as negative.
Compute each area A_i and its centroid (x_i, y_i).
Form Σ A_i x_i and Σ A_i y_i.
Divide each sum by total area Σ A_i to get x̄ and ȳ.

blocks.text: The second moment of area about an axis measures how far the area is spread from that axis. About the x-axis it is I_x = ∫ y² dA. Here y is the perpendicular distance from the axis in mm, dA is an area element in mm², and I_x is in mm⁴. A larger I means a stiffer section in bending. Some syllabi call this quantity moment of inertia; it is not mass moment of inertia because no mass appears.

For an axis through the centroid, write I_c. The parallel-axis theorem moves I from a centroidal axis to any parallel axis: I = I_c + A d². Here A is the area in mm², d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes in mm, and d² makes the shift positive either way. The theorem fails if the reference axis is not parallel or if I_c is not about the centroid.

blocks.where: I is the second moment about the required axis in mm⁴; I_c is about the centroidal axis parallel to it in mm⁴; A is area in mm²; d is the perpendicular distance between axes in mm.

blocks.text: For perpendicular axes x and y in the plane of the area, and z normal to the plane through the same point, the perpendicular-axis theorem gives I_z = I_x + I_y. I_z is the polar second moment about that point. Use this for circular sections or for any area where two perpendicular I values are known.

Learn the standard results. For a rectangle of width b and depth h, about the centroidal axis parallel to b, I_c = b h³/12. For a circle of diameter d, about a diameter, I_c = π d⁴/64. For a triangle of base b and height h, about the centroidal axis parallel to the base, I_c = b h³/36. About the base, the rectangle value becomes b h³/3 by the parallel-axis theorem.

For an I-section or T-section, split into rectangles and follow the same order. Find the overall centroid first. Then take each rectangle's own I_c about its centroidal axis parallel to the neutral axis, add A d² to shift it to the overall centroid, and sum over all rectangles. Do not add A d² to a rectangle without its own I_c. In bending of a homogeneous beam, the neutral axis passes through the centroid, so this I is the I used in M/I = σ/y, where M is bending moment, σ is bending stress, and y is distance from the neutral axis; see 4.2. The same I leads to section modulus in 4.3.

figure.caption: The section is split into rectangles, the overall centroid is found from first moments, and each rectangle is shifted to the neutral axis with I + A d².

spec.title: I by parts
spec.aria: Flowchart: split a section into rectangles, find each area and centroid, locate the overall centroid, apply the parallel-axis theorem, and sum to get the second moment of area about the neutral axis.

examples.question: A T-section has a flange 120 mm wide and 20 mm deep and a web 20 mm thick and 80 mm deep, so the total depth is 100 mm. Find the centroid from the bottom and the second moment of area about the horizontal centroidal axis.
steps: Set y upward from the bottom. Split the T into a top flange rectangle and a bottom web rectangle.
Flange area A_f = 120 × 20 = 2400 mm². Web area A_w = 20 × 80 = 1600 mm². Total area A = 2400 + 1600 = 4000 mm².
Flange centroid height y_f = 100 - 20/2 = 90 mm. Web centroid height y_w = 80/2 = 40 mm.
Centroid: ȳ = 280000 / 4000 = 70.0 mm from the bottom.
Flange own I about its centroid: I_fc = 120 × 20³ / 12 = 80000 mm⁴. Shift d_f = 90 - 70 = 20 mm. A_f d_f² = 2400 × 20² = 960000 mm⁴. Flange contribution = 80000 + 960000 = 1040000 mm⁴.
Web own I about its centroid: I_wc = 20 × 80³ / 12 = 853333.3 mm⁴. Shift d_w = 40 - 70 = -30 mm. A_w d_w² = 1600 × 30² = 1440000 mm⁴. Web contribution = 853333.3 + 1440000 = 2293333.3 mm⁴.
Total I about the horizontal centroidal axis = 1040000 + 2293333.3 = 3333333.3 mm⁴.
examples.answer: The centroid is 70.0 mm from the bottom and the second moment of area about the horizontal centroidal axis is 3,333,333.3 mm⁴, about 3.333 × 10⁶ mm⁴.
examples.check:
A_f = 120 * 20
A_w = 20 * 80
A = A_f + A_w
y_f = 100 - 20 / 2
y_w = 80 / 2
y_bar = (A_f * y_f + A_w * y_w) / A
I_fc = 120 * 20**3 / 12
I_f = I_fc + A_f * (y_f - y_bar)**2
I_wc = 20 * 80**3 / 12
I_w = I_wc + A_w * (y_w - y_bar)**2
I = I_f + I_w
print(round(y_bar, 1))
print(round(I, 1))

traps: Measuring ȳ from the top when dimensions are given from the bottom, or the reverse. The centroid stays in the same place, but the number changes (70 mm from the bottom is 30 mm from the top). Always say which edge ȳ is measured from.
Using d to the wrong axis in I = I_c + A d². The d must be between the part centroid and the required axis, perpendicular to both.
Forgetting each rectangle's own I_c and adding only A d². A rectangle has its own b h³/12 even when shifted.
Mixing first moment (mm³) with second moment (mm⁴), or using area in m² with lengths in mm.
Taking a T-section centroid at mid-depth. For the usual T with a wider flange, ȳ lies closer to the flange, not at 50 mm.

quiz.q: Define the centroid of a plane area.
quiz.a: The centroid is the point at which the first moment of area about any axis through it is zero; a thin uniform sheet of the shape would balance there.

quiz.q: Why does the parallel-axis theorem add A d² and not A d?
quiz.a: The second moment involves distance squared. Shifting the axis by d adds A d² to the centroidal value, so the correction is positive and has units of length to the fourth.

quiz.q: A rectangle is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep. Find I about the centroidal axis parallel to the width, and about the base.
quiz.a: I_c = b h³/12 = 100 × 200³/12 = 66.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴. About the base, I = b h³/3 = 266.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

quiz.q: A T-section has a wide flange at the top and a narrow web below. Explain why its centroid is above mid-depth.
quiz.a: The wide flange has more area far from the base, so the first moment sum is pulled upward. Dividing by total area gives a centroid closer to the flange than to the bottom.

quiz.q: Find the second moment of area of a circle of diameter 60 mm about a diameter.
State one difference between the first moment of area and the second moment of area.
quiz.a: The first moment is Q = Σ A y (or ∫ y dA); it locates the centroid and has unit mm³. The second moment is I = ∫ y² dA over the area; for a composite of finite parts it is I = Σ (I_c + A d²), with I_c the part's own second moment about its centroidal axis parallel to the required axis. Its unit is mm⁴.

quiz.q: Two sections have the same area. One is a solid rectangle; the other is an I-section with most material in the flanges. Which has the larger I about the horizontal centroidal axis, and why?
quiz.a: The I-section has the larger I. Its material lies farther from the neutral axis, and second moment weights each area element by the square of that distance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Section-property calculators in CAD and finite-element software compute centroid and second moment of area for arbitrary shapes by meshing the area, but the same two ideas remain the output that a beam solver uses. Optimisation of I-sections for a target I with minimum area is a standard structural-design problem. Composite and built-up sections need the parallel-axis theorem part by part.
